name: marcelcases/simd (std::experimental::simd kernels)
baseline: scalar C++ version of each kernel built with compiler auto-vectorization disabled (-fno-tree-vectorize)
workload: Seven exercises (nine kernel rows: element-wise add, memory-bound FMA, sum reduction, dot product, upper-bound clamp, count above threshold, stable softmax, horizontal blur, 1D convolution) written with libstdc++ std::experimental::simd versus scalar versions; 16,777,216 floats for the first four, 4,194,304 for softmax, a 1920x1080 grayscale image for blur, 1,048,576 floats for convolution; median of 9 samples.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+, one pinned core, GCC 14.1: sum reduction 5.37x, 1D convolution 5.89x, upper-bound clamp 6.81x, count above threshold 4.85x, horizontal blur 2.12x, dot product 1.78x, element-wise add 1.62x, softmax 1.57x, memory-bound FMA 1.04x. icpx 2025.2 on the same CPU: clamp 10.29x, dot product 4.45x, sum reduction 5.32x. Apple M1 Pro, GCC 15.2.0: count above threshold 24.51x, clamp 20.00x, sum reduction 4.00x, 1D convolution 4.02x, element-wise add 2.60x. Banana Pi F3 (RVV 1.0, VL=8): sum reduction 4.51x, 1D convolution 2.15x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.1 (MareNostrum 5), icpx 2025.2, Homebrew GCC 15.2.0 (M1), conda-forge GCC 16.2 cross-compiler (RISC-V); Makefile flags -std=c++2b -O3 -march=native -fno-math-errno -fno-trapping-math (plus -mavx512f/vl/dq/bw on x86); scalar builds add -fno-tree-vectorize -fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ (MareNostrum 5 GPP, one pinned core, exclusive node); Banana Pi F3 (RISC-V RVV 1.0, 256-bit VLEN); Apple M1 Pro (4-lane NEON, not pinned)
tradeoffs: Needs a C++23 compiler with libstdc++ <experimental/simd> (GCC); does not use C++26 <simd>. Makefile defaults target MareNostrum 5 AVX-512 and Apple M1, not generic hosts. Portable across x86-64, AArch64 and RISC-V RVV, but the RISC-V toolchain reports one lane for native_simd<float>, so fixed widths 4 and 8 were used.
caveats: Teaching study, not a reusable library. The baseline is deliberately de-vectorized scalar code, so the speedups say little about beating a normally compiled -O3 build. Element-wise add and memory-bound FMA are memory-traffic-limited (1.04x to 1.65x). The README itself notes that count_above on RISC-V contained no RVV instructions (gain is scalar unrolling), that icpx vectorizes softmax's exp loop through SVML, and that the large M1 clamp/count gains come from replacing branches with masks. x86 exercises 1-5 used three initial warm-ups instead of per-sample warm-ups and have not been refreshed. M1 run had no core pinning. Repository history starts 2026-09-03, so results are unreviewed.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/simd-programming?l=c++ and a WebSearch result titled 'SIMD instruction benchmark' led to the std::experimental::simd exercise repo; numbers read from its README

name: qReverse
workload: In-place reversal of arrays of 8 to 1,000,000 elements using byte-swap, SSSE3/NEON, AVX2 and AVX-512BW shuffle kernels, 10,000 trials per array size averaged.
claimed_speedup: README table (serial = x1): i9-7900X bswap x15.386, SSSE3 x10.417, AVX2 x22.032, AVX512 x22.357; i3-6100 bswap x15.8, SSSE3 x10.5, AVX2 x16.053; i5-8600K bswap x15.905, SSSE3 x10.21, AVX2 x16.076; E5-2697 v4 bswap x16.701, SSSE3 x15.716, AVX2 x19.141; Raspberry Pi BCM2837 (NEON) bswap x7.391, NEON x7.718. Detail, i3-6100: 100000 elements std::reverse 27511 ns vs qReverse 1739 ns (15.820x), 1000 elements 290 ns vs 36 ns (8.056x), 8 elements 19 ns vs 19 ns (1.000x), 1,000,000 elements 11.312x. Detail, i9-7900X AVX-512: 10000 elements 2504 ns vs 112 ns (22.357x).
compiler_and_flags: i3-6100 run: g++ -m64 -Ofast -march=native; i9-7900X AVX-512 run: Visual Studio 2017 x64 Release
hardware: Intel Core i3-6100 (8 GB DDR4), Core i9-7900X, Core i5-8600K, Xeon E5-2697 v4, Broadcom BCM2837 (Raspberry Pi)
tradeoffs: Per-architecture intrinsic kernels (SSSE3, AVX2, AVX-512BW, NEON) plus a bswap-based path; treats elements as raw bytes, so only suitable for trivially copyable element types. Headers only (include/), CMake build.
caveats: Numbers are from 2018 and older compilers (VS2017, an unstated g++ version, -Ofast). Benchmark source (tests/benchmark.cpp) is in the repo but the README's tables were not regenerated by a CI harness. No gain below about 16 elements and speedups fall for out-of-cache arrays (11x at 1M elements). libstdc++ versus MSVC STL is inferred from the compiler named for each run; the README does not say which standard library was linked. The std::reverse baseline is serial and not compared with a modern compiler-vectorized reversal.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/simd (C++, page 3 of the stars-sorted list) led to the Wunkolo repo; the README speedup tables and benchmark sections were read directly

name: CAFS (cache-aware frequency sort)
baseline: Google Highway vqsort (also compared: pdqsort, IPS4o, ska_sort, std::sort)
workload: Sorting integer arrays with few distinct values (K much smaller than N) over a 1600-point (N, K) grid, 592,770 measurements, using one AVX2 compare per element on 64-byte cache-line buckets.
claimed_speedup: Bin-mean speedup over vqsort 1.27x to 2.34x across the K << N band (1.32x at K 4-8, 1.27x at K 32-64, 2.34x at K 512-1024, 1.59x at K 8192-16384, 1.01x at K 131072-262144), also 1.7-3.1x over pdqsort, 1.97-3.52x over IPS4o, 4-17x over ska_sort and 8-17x over std::sort. vqsort wins past K = 6.7e5 (CAFS ratio 0.73 at K 524288-1048576 and 0.60 at K 8.4e6-1.7e7).
hardware: Intel Core i5-12400F, 32 GB DDR4-3200, Windows 11
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, x86-64 with AVX2 and BMI only; an adaptive dispatcher falls back to pdqsort or std::sort when the estimated distinct count K is large (K_est * 2 > N). Only pays off for low-cardinality integer columns.
caveats: Author-run benchmark; the accompanying preprint (arXiv 2605.25040 as cited in the README, not opened here) is not peer reviewed. Highway version and its dispatched target are not stated in the README (a 12400F has no AVX-512, so vqsort ran on AVX2 or lower). vqsort is faster than CAFS for high-cardinality inputs, so the headline range holds only for K << N. Repository history starts 2026-05-09. Single machine, Windows build.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/avx2?l=c++ page 2 listing (cafs-lib: cache-aware frequency sort for low-cardinality integer arrays); README results table with vqsort column

name: ParallelReductionsBenchmark
workload: Summing a 1 GB float or double array with hand-unrolled loops, AVX2, AVX-512, OpenMP, std::reduce with execution policies, Thrust, CUB and CUDA kernels, reported in bytes/s.
claimed_speedup: AWS Zen4 m7a.metal-48xl, GCC 12, single thread: unrolled<f32> 35.1514 GB/s and avx2<f32> 33.3195 GB/s versus std::accumulate<f32> 4.88655 GB/s (about 7.2x and 6.8x, derived from page data); avx512<f32interleaving> 26.8351 GB/s; multithreaded std::reduce<par,f32> 368.528 GB/s (about 75x, derived from page data). Nvidia DGX-H100 host, GCC 12: avx2<f32> 9.69112 GB/s versus std::accumulate<f32> 5.5322 GB/s (about 1.75x, derived from page data); cub@cuda 3.012 TB/s.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12 (NVCC 12.1 for CUDA); CMakeLists.txt sets -O2 -march=native -fopenmp for GCC
hardware: AWS m7a.metal-48xl (AMD Zen4, 192 threads listed at 3701.95 MHz) and an Nvidia DGX-H100 node (160 threads listed at 2100 MHz); CPU model strings are not named in the README
tradeoffs: Educational benchmark harness rather than a drop-in library. Hand-written AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels are x86 only; NEON and SVE variants exist for Arm. Huge pages, NUMA and Kahan summation are handled by hand.
caveats: No LICENSE file found (raw LICENSE, LICENSE.md, LICENSE.txt and COPYING all return 404), so the code is reference only. CPU models are given by instance type, not model name, which is why this is tier C. The error% column shows that plain float accumulation of 1 GB is inaccurate (std::accumulate<f32> 93.75% error, unrolled<f32> 50%); only f64 and Kahan rows are accurate, and the avx2<f32kahan> row is only about 2x faster than std::accumulate<f32> on Zen4. The README's own conclusion is that multithreaded std::reduce is the CPU winner, not SIMD alone. Numbers are the author's single runs.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/sve (C++ list) surfaced the repo; README result tables for DGX-H100 and AWS Zen4 read directly

name: glam
baseline: cgmath and nalgebra (scalar Rust linear algebra crates, as measured by mathbench)
workload: mathbench-rs Criterion micro-benchmarks of 3D game math (matrix4 inverse, transpose, determinant, multiply, vector3 cross/dot/normalize) on f32 data, with glam using SSE2 for Vec3A, Vec4, Quat, Mat2, Mat3A and Mat4.
claimed_speedup: mathbench scalar table, Ryzen 7 3800X, glam 0.34.1: matrix4 inverse 12.1455 ns vs cgmath 30.8124 ns and nalgebra 40.8410 ns (about 2.5x and 3.4x, derived from page data); matrix4 transpose 2.7248 ns vs 7.6718 ns and 7.7156 ns (about 2.8x); matrix4 determinant 4.3934 ns vs 7.1764 ns and 40.9609 ns; vector3 cross 1.0511 ns vs 1.5374 ns and 1.5364 ns; matrix4 mul matrix4 4.4589 ns vs 6.2970 ns and 4.7309 ns. Not faster everywhere: matrix4 mul vector4 x1 2.1002 ns vs nalgebra 1.9185 ns and cgmath 1.9625 ns; matrix2 mul matrix2 1.1531 ns vs cgmath 1.1030 ns.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28), default cargo bench profile, command 'cargo bench --features scalar scalar'
tradeoffs: 128-bit SIMD storage on x86, x86_64, aarch64 and wasm32 for Vec3A, Vec4, Quat, Mat2, Mat3A, Mat4, Affine2 and Affine3A (SSE2 default on x86_64, NEON default on aarch64); padded Vec3A/Mat3A waste space. Rust only; usable from C++ only through FFI.
caveats: mathbench is written by glam's author, so the shootout is not independent. Default bench profile is used (no target-cpu=native), so SIMD benefit is limited to SSE2 width. The glam README itself gives no numbers and says wasm SIMD has not been benchmarked. Several rows are ties within 2.5% or small losses.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/simd (Rust) list showed bitshifter/glam-rs; the mathbench-rs README is the shootout whose scalar-table winners were harvested

name: ultraviolet
baseline: glam single-lane types (glam_f32x1) in mathbench; nalgebra wide types tie
workload: mathbench-rs 'wide' benchmarks processing batches of 16 to 80000 elements with structure-of-arrays f32x4 and f32x8 types: euler rotations, ray-sphere intersection, matrix4 determinant/inverse/multiply, vector3 cross/dot/normalize.
claimed_speedup: mathbench wide table, Ryzen 7 3800X, RUSTFLAGS -C target-feature=+avx2: ultraviolet_f32x8 vs glam_f32x1: euler 2d x80000 18.94 us vs 41.87 us (about 2.2x), euler 3d x80000 28.54 us vs 58.97 us, ray-sphere intersection x80000 25.26 us vs 497.6 us (about 20x), matrix4 determinant x16 14.6545 ns vs 62.0342 ns (about 4.2x), vector3 normalize x16 7.3365 ns vs 35.2002 ns (about 4.8x), all ratios derived from page data. nalgebra_f32x8 is equal or within noise (euler 2d 18.57 us).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28), RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+avx2' cargo bench --features wide wide; ultraviolet 0.10.0
tradeoffs: Requires an SoA/AoSoA data layout (wide f32x4 and f32x8 types) rather than ordinary Vec3 structs; AVX2 must be enabled explicitly at build time. Rust only.
caveats: The comparison is against glam's one-lane scalar-in-a-wide-table type, so the large ratios mostly measure SoA batching, not a better library; nalgebra's f32x8 types match ultraviolet. In mathbench's scalar table ultraviolet wins only the matrix2 and matrix3 transpose rows. The ray-sphere ratio (about 20x for 4-8 lanes) suggests the glam_f32x1 path is unusually slow on that row. mathbench is written by glam's author. No LICENSE file found at common names; the MIT OR Apache-2.0 OR Zlib expression is from Cargo.toml (HEAD is 0.11.0, benchmark used 0.10.0).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/simd (Rust) list; the ultraviolet README points to mathbench-rs for benchmarks, whose wide table was read

name: faster (Rust SIMD iterators)
workload: A cargo bench map over a slice, scalar iterator versus faster's SIMD iterator, built for ivybridge (AVX), x86-64 (SSE2) and pentium (polyfill only) targets.
claimed_speedup: target-cpu=ivybridge (AVX): map_scalar 6,963 ns/iter vs map_simd 879 ns/iter (about 7.9x, derived from page data); target-cpu=x86-64 (SSE2): 7,237 ns/iter vs 1,879 ns/iter (about 3.9x); target-cpu=pentium (polyfills): 7,195 ns/iter vs 6,271 ns/iter.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=ivybridge' / 'x86-64' / 'pentium'; rustc version not stated
hardware: host is ivybridge (only stated in README comments); exact CPU model not given
tradeoffs: Iterator-style SIMD abstraction for Rust with polyfills for CPUs lacking the target feature; depends on packed_simd_2 (nightly-era API). Not usable from C++ without FFI.
caveats: The README calls its own benchmarks 'extremely unscientific'. The benchmark source and what map computes are not shown on the README page, rustc version is unstated, and the numbers are from a single ivybridge host. Last commit 2021-03-25 and the project depends on the old packed_simd_2 crate, so it may not build on current stable Rust.
